text: Given a string s, rearrange its characters so that no two adjacent characters are the same. Return any valid rearrangement, or return an empty string if it's not possible.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I have to use every character exactly once. I can only reorder them. And if there are many valid answers, any one is fine?
Yes. Any valid answer is accepted.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
The length of s is between one and five hundred, and s has only lowercase English letters.

Okay. So there are at most twenty-six different letters — a small, fixed number. Before any code, I want to know when it's possible. Say the most common letter shows up max freq times. Every two copies of it need another letter between them, so the best I can do is positions zero, two, four, and so on. That gives n plus one over two slots. So it's possible exactly when max freq is at most n plus one over two. Quick check: A A B has length three and two A's, which fits, so A B A works. A A A B has three A's but only two slots, so I return an empty string.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to try every order of the characters and return the first one with no two equal neighbors. That's up to n factorial orders — hopeless for n up to five hundred. This problem reminds me of greedy scheduling with a max-heap. The letter with the most copies left is the one in the most danger, so I should use it as early and as often as I'm allowed. I'll take two letters per round: the most common, then the second most common. They come from two different heap entries, so they're different letters. Then I put both back with one less copy.

Here's the plan. One: count each letter and push every count with its letter into a max-heap. Two: each round, pop up to two letters, most common first, and append them. Three: push back each one that still has copies left. One thing worth flagging — where can two equal letters end up next to each other? Inside one round, never: the two letters are different heap entries. Between rounds, maybe: the last letter of one round can match the first letter of the next. So I only check that seam — right after adding the first letter, compare the last two characters, and if they match, return empty. There's a trade-off: an up-front formula check also works; the loop check needs no formula, but finds out late. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I count the letters, fill a max-heap, then loop: pop the top, append it, check the seam, pop a second letter if one is left, and push back whatever still has copies. The order matters here — I pop the second letter before I push the first one back. If I pushed it back first, it could come right back out as the second letter, and I'd place the same letter twice in a row. One thing worth flagging — the seam check is size at least two, not greater than two. The very first seam is at size two, so it has to be included. I'll come back to this in the review.

Let's dry-run the code with A A A B B C — three A's in six letters, exactly at the limit. The key round is round two: the last letter is B and the top is A, so the seam is safe. Then C pops before B, because on equal counts the larger letter wins in a pair max-heap. The result is A B A C B A — no equal neighbors. Corner cases: a single letter returns itself. A A B B returns B A B A. V V V L O is right at the limit and works. And A A, the smallest impossible input, returns empty. That last one caught my first draft: with greater than two, the size-two seam was skipped and A A came back unchanged — and both official examples pass with that bug.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is O of n log twenty-six, which is linear: each character is popped once and pushed back at most once, and the heap never holds more than twenty-six entries, so each operation is constant. Space is twenty-six counters plus the heap, so constant extra, not counting the output. In the worst case, n is five hundred, so at most about a thousand heap operations. That's tiny.
Could you avoid the check inside the loop?

Yes. Check max freq greater than n plus one over two once at the start, and return empty. After that, the greedy never gets stuck, so the loop needs no check. But the formula must be exactly n plus one over two — with n over two, even A and A A B would wrongly return empty. The in-loop check works because of the pairing: inside a round, the two letters always differ, so the only place a repeat can appear is the seam, and one compare per round covers it. Oh, one more thing — the answer depends on tie-breaking. A pair of int and char puts the larger letter first on equal counts, so A A B B gives B A B A, not A B A B. That's fine here, but a test should check validity, not one exact string.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You stated the condition, max freq at most n plus one over two, before writing any code. You showed that taking two letters per round means only the seam between rounds needs checking. And you caught your own greater-than-two bug by testing A A, the smallest impossible input, which both official examples miss. Good work.
